rows.title: Monetary Policy
rows.figure: Fed Dec hike ~96% (CME FedWatch); Mar hike ~35%, from >50%; ECB Dec ~90%; BoE Dec ~84%; BoJ Dec ~84% (JPMorgan ~50%); BoC Dec ~44%
rows.read: Traders still fully expect a quarter-point Fed hike in December, though bets on further hikes into the spring have cooled a little. The Bank of England, European Central Bank and Bank of Japan are also expected to hike in December. The Fed still looks set to go furthest, which keeps the dollar on top.

rows.title: Growth
rows.figure: Japan Nov PMI mfg 53.7 (fcst 53.5), services 50.5 (Oct 51.7); US composite 54.6; Germany composite 55.0; France 46.2; UK 52.3; Ifo due 3:00 AM CT (fcst 90.6); US Q3 GDP 2nd est Wed (fcst 3.5%)
rows.read: Japan's factories picked up in November while its services slowed, echoing mixed surveys in the US and Europe on Monday. None of it has changed what central banks are expected to do. Coming up, Germany's Ifo survey and the second estimate of US growth.

rows.title: Inflation
rows.figure: Australia CPI Oct due Tue 6:30 PM CT (fcst 4.8% y/y, Sep 4.3%); US core PCE Oct due Wed 7:30 AM CT (fcst +0.3% m/m, 3.2% y/y); Tokyo core CPI Nov due Thu 5:30 PM CT (fcst 2.9%); Brent ~$88.5
rows.read: Inflation is still well above target almost everywhere, which keeps most central banks leaning toward hikes. Falling oil should ease some of that pressure in the months ahead. Australian inflation on Tuesday evening and US core inflation on Wednesday are the week's big tests.

rows.title: Risk Sentiment
rows.figure: S&P 500 ~+5%, Nasdaq ~+7% Mon (Hercules); USD/JPY ~159.06; USD/CHF ~0.8408; US 2-year ~4.72%
rows.read: Markets stayed calm overnight after Monday's big rally in US stocks. With little fear around, the yen and the franc got no safe-haven lift, and the dollar held up on interest rates instead. Fresh reports of attacks in the Gulf did not shake markets.

rows.title: Terms of Trade
rows.figure: Brent ~$88.47 (−0.9%), lowest close since Aug 31; WTI ~$79.28; gold ~$3,650; world oil stocks +52M bbl in Oct (Deutsche Bank)
rows.read: Oil kept sliding toward a three-month low as supply looks ample, which hurts the Canadian dollar and helps oil importers like the euro area and Japan. Gold held most of its rebound, giving the Aussie a little support.

rows.title: Positioning
rows.figure: Hedge funds (CFTC, Nov 17): USD index −1.3K (flipped short), EUR −76.6K, GBP +28.8K, JPY −23.8K, CHF −19.8K, CAD −72.1K, AUD +38.0K, NZD −23.6K; asset managers GBP −104.6K, AUD −182.7K, EUR +147.2K
rows.read: The latest weekly figures show hedge funds have turned slightly against the dollar, while still betting against the euro, the kiwi, the franc and, most strongly, the Canadian dollar. They still bet on the pound and the Aussie, where big long-term investors take the opposite side. Where the two groups disagree, a surprise could set off a fast unwind.

rows.title: Fiscal
rows.figure: US 10-year near 5% (Hercules); France composite PMI 46.2, a six-month low; ECB Financial Stability Review: France debt 119% of GDP, deficit 5.5%
rows.read: France's debts weigh more now that its economy looks close to recession. Heavy US government borrowing keeps long-term US borrowing costs near 5%, which supports the dollar's yield but raises questions about debt over time.
